assets.content:
Subject: Is that signup spike real?
Preview text: A raw count can't tell you — a goal measured against filtered visits can.

Hi there,

After a signup burst, the number you judge it by is the raw total.

That total counts whatever reached the page — bots, referrer spam and data-center traffic included. So the conversion rate you work out from it may not reflect real people.

Plausible is a privacy-friendly web analytics dashboard. It excludes bots, referrer spam and data-center traffic out of the box, so the visits it counts are real human ones.

Set your trial signup as a goal, and the dashboard reports that goal's conversion rate against those filtered visits — along with the referrer sources and entry pages driving each signup. One total becomes a breakdown of where real signups come from.

The official goal-conversions guide walks through setting up a signup goal, or reviewing one you already have. That is the concrete first step before any of it shows up for your own site.

Read the goal-conversions guide →

- the Plausible Analytics team

P.S. The guide explains how goals work; seeing your own numbers takes Plausible running on your site.

reader_verdicts.relevance_feedback: Profile-supported: I measure visitor-to-signup conversion and care about spikes, so the 'is your spike real' framing lands on a job I actually do. Email-only premise: it assumes my current conversion number is distorted by bots/referrer spam and that I'm not already filtering them — the profile doesn't say what analytics I run. It also only touches the visitor-to-signup denominator; my documented trial-to-paid pain (including payment-method failures) is untouched here, but that's not a mismatch, just a narrower scope.

reader_verdicts.problem_now: Measuring signup conversion accurately is a live, documented concern for me, especially after a spike. But whether bot-inflated denominators are actually my problem is unknown — I may already have analytics that handles this. No deadline is established.

reader_verdicts.biggest_doubt: I likely already have some analytics in place, and the payoff here (a cleaner denominator) requires installing and running a new tool before I see anything — the email even admits that in the P.S. The effort-to-reward isn't obviously worth it three minutes before a meeting.
reader_verdicts.to_click_it_would_have_to: told me how much my conversion rate typically shifts once bot/spam traffic is removed — a real number or example — so I'd know whether this is a rounding error or the reason my numbers look off.

brief.arc: Single email: name the reader's question about understanding trial signups, show the one concrete first step (a signup goal), say what the dashboard then breaks out (sources, entry pages, conversion rate), answer the 'does this need code' hesitation, and send them to the official guide to set it up or review how theirs is configured.

emails.job: Introduce Plausible and get the reader to open the goal-conversions guide to set up or review a trial-signup goal.
emails.single_idea: If you define your trial signup as a goal in Plausible, the dashboard stops showing one signup total and starts showing which sources and landing pages drive those signups.
emails.felt_need: Free-trial signups do not convert to paid at a rate the owner considers acceptable, even after a signup surge.
emails.status_quo: They add free trials that require a payment method upfront to try to convert website visitors into paying customers.
emails.why_it_fails: One aggregate number has no breakdown by source or entry page, so every improvement to the signup flow is a guess that can't be attributed to anything.
emails.mechanism: You mark the trial registration as a goal — a pageview goal on the registration or confirmation page needs no code changes because pageviews are collected automatically — and once it's recording, that goal reports its conversion rate alongside the referrer sources and the entry pages that drive conversions.
